Real weight came in 1958, when Batista launched Operation Verano (June–August 1958) with some 10,000 troops and air support and it collapsed: at Jigüe (11–21 July 1958) Che Guevara's column encircled and captured over 200 soldiers, and the rebels then carried the war west in August 1958 through the columns of Che (to Las Villas) and Camilo Cienfuegos (to Pinar del Río), culminating at Santa Clara, where on 29 December 1958 bulldozers derailed Batista's armoured train and some 300 troops surrendered.\n\nThat a few hundred guerrillas defeated a 30,000–40,000-man army with American equipment is inexplicable in purely tactical terms, which is why the thesis must centre Batista. His officer corps was chosen for loyalty rather than competence — the Tabernilla family's grip on the high command is the classic example — conscripts were unmotivated, coordination between columns failed, and the army's indiscriminate violence in the Sierra drove peasants into rebel arms. Answering the research question: guerrilla tactics were necessary but not sufficient. What made the *foco* viable was Batista's inability to use his own superiority, and the contingency school therefore explains the outcome through regime failure rather than through the inherent genius of guerrilla method.\n\n---\n\n**Batista's weaknesses**\n\nThis is the causal core of the essay, and here the thesis and the school of thought converge most tightly. The contingency school argues that Batista manufactured his own defeat through a sequence of choices, and the chronology supports it. He seized power in the coup of 10 March 1952, cancelling the scheduled elections and destroying his legitimacy at the outset; he then \"won\" the election of 1 November 1954 against a withdrawn opposition. His regime rested on a casino economy personified by Meyer Lansky's Havana Riviera (1957), on padded army payrolls, and on torture and informers. Each act of repression created martyrs — above all Frank País (30 July 1957) — and each rigged election created recruits for the armed opposition. The presidential election of 3 November 1958, in which Andrés Rivero Agüero ran while the opposition abstained, was transparently fraudulent and convinced Washington that Batista could not be saved.\n\nMilitarily his weaknesses were equally self-inflicted: he distrusted his own officers, relying on the SIM intelligence apparatus and on micro-management, and he refused to arm peasant militias that might have countered the guerrillas. When Operation Verano failed in August 1958, the army's morale never recovered, and when Batista fled to the Dominican Republic on 1 January 1959 the regime dissolved within hours as General Cantillo's coup at Camp Columbia confirmed that the army had been held together only by his person. Answering the research question: Batista's weaknesses were not merely one factor among five but the catalyst operating on all of them — the illegitimacy that made propaganda credible, the poor command that made guerrilla tactics viable, the repression that attracted international criticism, and the fraud that finally fractured the opposition into a single front. Structuralists would say the 1952 coup was itself a symptom of deeper crisis, and the essay concedes this; but even a structural crisis required a Batista to detonate it.\n\n---\n\n**Support from other countries**\n\nExternal support is where the thesis is most strongly vindicated, because the decisive feature of 1956–58 is how little of it the rebels had. The United States, far from backing Castro, armed Batista: Cuba received American military assistance under the Mutual Defense Assistance agreement from 1952 and purchased aircraft and munitions throughout the 1950s. Only when Batista's illegitimacy became an American embarrassment did Washington move — Ambassador Earl E. T. Smith, arriving in June 1957, pressed for clean elections, the arms embargo of 14 March 1958 suspended further shipments, and in December 1958 the William Pawley mission was sent to persuade Batista to step down. That shift was not a cause of Batista's weakness but a consequence of it. The Soviet Union, meanwhile, gave the rebels nothing: the Popular Socialist Party followed Moscow's \"peaceful coexistence\" line and dismissed Castro's *foco* as adventurism, and Soviet–Cuban relations were only established in 1960, after Mikoyan's visit. Castro won without Soviet aid, which is fatal to any Cold War school that explains 1959 through superpower intervention.\n\nLatin American support was similarly marginal: Mexico tolerated the purchase and fitting-out of the *Granma* in 1956 and then arrested the conspirators, and Venezuela and other states recognised the new government only after 1 January 1959. Answering the research question: international factors were secondary and derivative. Batista's collapse caused his American patron to abandon him, and the absence of Soviet backing proves that Castro's victory was not produced from outside. Armed unity then failed too: Echeverría's assault on the Presidential Palace on 13 March 1957 killed him and showed that individual heroism could not topple the regime, and the general strike of 9 April 1958 collapsed within days, discrediting the urban underground leadership and shifting weight decisively to the Sierra.
